Collective Falsification

Every agent in a population starts with the same wrong rule. Each can run a few experiments and tell its neighbours what it found. Does the population find its error?

By Artem Zvyagintsev, who designed, ran and analysed the experiments · github.com/corba777

The question that started this track was raised by Michal Valko (Isara Labs and Inria), who also proposed the comparison in entry 4.

Why this question

In a group where everyone holds the same belief, the evidence against it often reaches only one member. Human groups are known to handle this badly. In the hidden-profile studies (Stasser and Titus, 1985), groups spend their discussion on what everyone already knows and seldom bring out what only one member knows, even when that decides the answer.

Populations of language-model agents face the same problem whenever the agents see different data. This page measures it step by step: does an agent find the counterexample, change its own mind, pass the evidence on, and do its neighbours act on it?

The tests are one-sided exact permutation tests on per-run means, four runs or worlds against four (70 splits), or a sign test over worlds; α = 0.05 per claim. Sample sizes are small: four or five runs per condition.

What is observed

Counted after the data, or from one run per condition. These are not tests.

  • Two pieces of evidence, found by different cells. For Luna at δ = 1/64, the true rule was usually put together from a rare counterexample against the starting rule and a common negative result against its simpler rival U, found by different cells (entry 8).
  • Test guidance. A Luna cell with four tests that had heard the true rule named put 84 % of its tests where that rule differs from the starting one, against 3.7 % for a cell that had not (entry 9). That the name causes the choice of test has not been tested. gpt-oss-20b shows the same pattern with one test per cell: with names, more tests on the region and more finders than in silence, in every world (entry 15).
  • Five models, five profiles (entries 1, 2, 11–14, 19–23). Luna passes evidence on and follows a majority of names. gpt-oss-20b attaches a result to about 2 % of its messages and is not moved by names, but the few results it sends move neighbours. gpt-oss-120b talks almost every turn, nearly always a rule name, sends 0–2 counterexamples per run, and those carry the whole of its spread beyond the finders; its recovery at δ = 1/8 (0.10–0.13) is in gpt-oss-20b's range. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, under a thinking budget, hardly tests, never sends a result, and is silent in 60–64 % of its turns; nothing spreads. Claude Haiku 5.5 (entry 19) is the first model from outside OpenAI that ran without trouble: names alone moved almost no cell (x̄nf ≤ 0.004), and the few results it sent carried HT to most of the grid, so spread beyond the finders is not an OpenAI-only property. Nemotron failed the format gate in three runs and is not run further; Gemma 4 31B takes its place. A capped-thinking run of Qwen3.6 is pending.
  • Spreading a refutation is not identifying the rule. At δ = 1/64 a single counterexample fits both HT and the simpler unconditional substitution. When the engine attached Haiku's counterexample to every message, 94–97 cells left HF and 81–88 of them took the substitution (entry 22); across worlds, every Haiku finder took it too (entry 23). Luna reached HT in the same setting from two results found by different cells: the counterexample and a result the substitution gets wrong (entry 8). With four tests per cell Haiku reached HT too (entry 24, W-H4E held): 129 of 189 cells that got there held a received counterexample and a result against the substitution from their own tests. Counted after the data.
  • The majority step differs by model. Take a cell on HF with no counterexample of its own or received, at the first generation in which one to four, or five or more, of its eight neighbours named another rule (the definition of entry 7), and ask whether it leaves HF then. Luna: 2 of 356 and 187 of 208. gpt-oss-20b: 1 of 55 at five or more (entry 11). Claude Haiku 5.5: 0 of 497 and 0 of 60 (its rule-only runs in entries 19 and 20, and the four cells of entry 21). Ten Haiku cells did leave, each only after 3 to 16 generations with five or more naming neighbours.

What is open

  • Where each model's bottleneck is. One cell at a time, the same counterexample given as its own or as a neighbour's (entry 16): Luna and gpt-oss-120b update on their own and less often on a received one; gpt-oss-20b updates on half of either and rarely passes the evidence on; Qwen3.6, with its thinking capped, updates on most of either, more when the sender names HT, and passes its own counterexample on in about three updating answers of four; Nemotron was stopped by the format gate.
  • Family or capability. Claude Haiku 5.5 answered part of it: it has now run every core experiment (entries 16 and 19–24). Of the open models from other families, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has run isolation with a capped thinking budget (entry 16); Gemma 4 31B, which replaces Nemotron, is deferred. gpt-oss-120b is running the two population experiments it lacks.
  • Why gpt-oss-20b keeps its evidence. Its reasoning is stored for every call and is being coded, with the coding instructions fixed on a pilot run before the main runs are read.
  • Whether a name causes the choice of test, and whether cells pick informative tests at all: a measure of the information each chosen test carries about the rules a cell still holds possible, fixed before computing.
  • Scope. One task family with a listed true rule, so the agents choose rather than invent it; one prompt; up to five worlds.

The world

The world, prompt, outcomes and scripted references were fixed before any model call (QX-2 phase 1 amendment). Every later experiment on this page uses it unchanged.

  • Strings and rules. Inputs are four letters from A–H, so there are 4,096 of them. A rule maps an input to an output.
  • The false rule HF is shift_symbols(1), which moves every letter one step forward. Every cell holds it at the start.
  • The true rule HT is HF followed by one substitution, so the two disagree on a share δ of the inputs. The substitutions below are those of world seed 0. Entries 8–10 and 13 also use worlds 1–4, where the seed draws another substitution, other examples, keys and catalog order; their entries give each world’s rule.
    • δ = 1/8 (control): shift_symbols(1);subst(0,E,F). On input DAAA, HF gives EBBB and HT gives FBBB.
    • δ = 1/64 (main): shift_symbols(1);subst_if(0,E,F,1,H). It only differs when the input starts with DG.
    Why two values: at δ = 1/8 one random test in eight exposes the error, so finding it is easy and the open question is whether it spreads. At δ = 1/64 a random test almost never does, so finding it is itself the hard step. The common error is the control, the rare one the main case.
  • Private evidence. Each cell has two examples. All of them lie on inputs where HF and HT agree, so no cell can see the error from its examples alone. The error can only be found by testing.
  • The catalog. It has 117 rules: the 101 base rules of the Life world, plus 16 substitution variants in four clusters. One counterexample still leaves at least two rules that fit, so finding HT takes more than one test. Because the true rule is listed, an agent never has to invent it, only to tell it apart from its neighbours in the catalog.
  • Experiments. A cell has a budget of B tests, at most one per generation. It names an input and gets the true output one generation later. Only that cell sees the result. The cell chooses when to spend a test and on which input; once its B tests are spent it has none left for the rest of the run. No test is offered in the last generation, because its result could not arrive. With B = 1 a cell gets exactly one attempt to find a counterexample. Because only the tester sees its result, a counterexample stays private evidence until the cell chooses to put it in a message.
  • Messages. 100 cells sit on a 10 × 10 torus and each hears its 8 neighbours. A message is seen by the neighbours in the next generation. What it may carry depends on the entry:
    • rule, result or nothing (entries 1–3, 12, 14): the key of the rule the cell holds, or one result from its memory, its own or relayed, never both, or nothing;
    • rule, plus a result (entries 4–9, 11, 13): always the rule; in the "chosen result" condition the cell may add one result, in the "attached result" condition the engine adds one; "rule only" carries no result;
    • no message delivered (entry 10): every message is dropped.
    A cell can only share a result it actually has, and the engine fills in the output, so every shared result is true. Messages also carry a number 0–7, carried over from the Life world, where it is the only channel; here it shows whether a model invents a marker for evidence. The run viewer shows the message mix for every generation of every run.
  • A run lasts 12 generations. The length was a convention, not derived from anything; entry 3 showed that rare-error runs need more, and entries 4–7 use 24. The outcomes are measured at generation 12:
    • abandonment is the share of cells no longer holding HF;
    • recovery is the share holding HT.

Reading

  1. The setup works. Every delivered result was a true output of HT, the engine checks held throughout, and no answer failed the format.
  2. Experiments are cheap but not used. With four tests per cell, the population spent 44–70 of 400. The tests cluster on a few patterns: about half start with A, and AAAA and ABCD are frequent.
  3. When the error is rare (δ = 1/64), it is not found. None of 44 tests hit an input starting with DG. A random tester with the same 44 tests would have hit one about half the time.
  4. When the error is common (δ = 1/8), it is found but not passed on. Tests hit refuting inputs two to four times more often than chance. Cells that found a counterexample almost always left HF: 79 of 84 did, and 54 reached HT. But they kept naming rules in their messages instead of sharing the evidence: 6 messages in four runs carried a refuting result, each from a different cell. Only 14 cells reached HT without a counterexample of their own.
  5. Evidence that is shared does work. The 6 shared counterexamples reached 30 neighbours that still held HF. Within two generations, 15 of them left HF and 11 reached HT. Among cells that saw no counterexample, own or shared, 2.2 % left HF within two generations, and 1.2 % reached HT. The numbers are small, and this comparison was made after seeing the data.
  6. The signal field drifts to 0. The generation-0 messages the cells first see carry signals drawn uniformly from 0–7. Yet already in generation 1, 57–68 % of messages carry 0, and in generations 10–12, 89–95 %. No value marks HT or shared results.
  7. So the process breaks at different steps. An agent has to choose a test, read the result, update its own rule, decide to share the result, and neighbours have to act on it. At δ = 1/64 it breaks at the first step: no test found the difference. At δ = 1/8 the first three steps work, the last works when it gets the chance, and the fourth almost never happens.
  8. The single agent is an upper bound, not a matched control. It holds the whole budget and sees every result itself, so it does not isolate the cost of spreading the work. The scripted references in the table above do part of that, with the same distributed setup and fixed sharing policies. With four tests per cell, the populations did no better than with one.

Extended runs (added 2026-11-24)

The four population runs at δ = 1/8 were still moving at generation 12, so they were continued to generation 24 in the same way as Luna's extended runs (entry 3): restored to generation 12 from the stored answers, then played on, with "24 generations" in the prompt from generation 13. These four runs were chosen after their data were seen, so the extension is descriptive.

Cells holding HT, of 100. In generations 13–24 cells sent a result in 13–16 messages per run (of about 1,200); a few cells moved to other rules of the catalog, shown as "another subst rule" in the viewer. One answer ran out of length and was drawn again.

With four tests per cell the share on HT kept rising, to 71–81 of 100; with one test it rose slowly or stopped, at 20–42. The extra generations gave cells with tests left more chances to find the error themselves; results were still rarely shared. Counted after the data.

Limits: one model, one world, one or two runs per condition, 12 generations (four runs extended to 24). All numbers are descriptive.

Recovery is the share of cells on HT at generation 12; the "20b" column gives the pilot's runs in the same cell. A random tester puts 1.6 % of its tests on δ-inputs at δ = 1/64 and 12.5 % at δ = 1/8. Finders are cells whose own test refuted HF. "Shared counterexamples" counts messages that carried a refuting result.

Reading

  1. Luna designs its experiments. Its first tests include DGHF, DCGF and DCHF, inputs that separate the substitution rules listed in the catalog. At δ = 1/64, 38 % of its tests landed on the rare inputs where the two rules differ. A random tester lands 1.6 %, and gpt-oss-20b landed 0 of 44.
  2. Every Luna finder adopts the true rule. All 195 cells whose own test refuted HF ended on HT. For 20b, 54 of 84 did.
  3. Luna shares the evidence. Each run carried 11–52 counterexamples to neighbours, from 9–44 different cells. Cells also pass on counterexamples they received: about half of the shared counterexamples are relays. In the rare-error cell with one test per agent, 5 agents found the error, 10 of the 11 shared counterexamples were relays, and 32 cells ended on the true rule, so 27 got it from others.
  4. Cells that did not find the error themselves were moved by evidence, not by rule names. Of the 136 Luna cells that ended on HT without a counterexample of their own, 133 had first seen one shared by a neighbour. The same holds for gpt-oss-20b, where 12 of 14 had. This comparison was made after seeing the data.
  5. Luna beats the scripted sharers. At δ = 1/64 with B = 4, it recovers 1.00. Scripted random testers that share refutations reach 0.61. The difference is the choice of tests.
  6. The signal field again carries no evidence. Luna's default is 7, where 20b's was 0. True-rule messages and shared counterexamples both carry 7, so no value marks evidence apart from rule names.

Limits: one run per cell, and the two δ arms at the same budget share their first generations. The catalog lists the true rule and its siblings, so this is testing within a given set of hypotheses, which is easier than finding an unlisted rule.

3 · Luna, second runs and extended runs

2026-11-15descriptive

Luna · δ 1/8 and 1/64 · B 1 and 4 · message: the rule, or one result, or nothing; one of the three, the cell chooses · 12 generations, some runs extended to 24 · world 0

Two follow-ups to entry 2, each fixed before its data. The first runs every cell a second time, with independent arms (second-run amendment). The second extends runs that were still moving at generation 12 to generation 24 (extension amendment).

  • Second runs. They use the same model, prompt and settings as entry 2, with a fresh cache keyed by arm, so no answer is reused.
  • Extended runs. A run is restored to generation 12 from its stored answers, and the restored rules, tests and messages equal the stored trace. It is then played on to generation 24. The prompt states the run length, so generations 1–12 were played under "12 generations" and the prompts from generation 13 on say "24". Each call sees only its own prompt.
    • Luna run 1 at δ 1/64, B 1 was chosen after its data were seen.
    • The second runs were extended by a rule fixed in advance: extend if 1–99 cells hold HT at generation 12, and more than at generation 9, that is, a run neither finished nor stalled. The rule selected both δ 1/64 cells and neither δ 1/8 cell.

Reading

  1. Given time, every rare-error Luna run reaches the whole population. The three extended runs reach 100 cells on HT by generation 16, 18 and 22. With one test per cell, the run that stood at 32 % at generation 12 was not stuck, only slow.
  2. The common-error cells replicate. In both runs, both budgets reach the ceiling within the first 6–10 generations.
  3. The rare-error cells vary between runs, in both directions. At B = 4, run 2 stood at 79 at generation 12 against 100 for run 1, and it shared half as many counterexamples (24 against 49) with similar test quality. At B = 1, run 2 stood at 55 against 32, with 9 finders against 5. With few finders, how many of them share decides the pace.
  4. Shared evidence still drives the converts. In the second runs, 131 of the 132 cells that reached HT by generation 12 without a counterexample of their own had first seen one shared by a neighbour. Over the whole of extended run 1 the share is lower: 70 of its 85 such cells. Late converts also follow rule names. This line was first found after seeing the data, and the second runs replicate it.
  5. The test budgets get used. By generation 24, 98–100 of the 100 cells at B = 1 have spent their test. Tests after generation 12 added 10–23 finders per run.

Limits: two runs per cell. The extended runs carry the splice at generation 12. The gpt-oss-20b runs from entry 1 are queued for the same extension.

4 · Rule alone against rule plus counterexample (Luna)

2026-11-16descriptive pilot

Luna · δ 1/64 · B 1 · message: rule only / rule + chosen result / rule + attached result · 24 generations · world 0 · a cell may also send nothing

Entries 1–3 found that cells which reach the true rule without a counterexample of their own had almost always seen one shared by a neighbour. That was noticed after the data were seen, and it does not show that the evidence causes the switch. Michal Valko proposed the test: compare sharing the rule alone with sharing the rule plus a counterexample, under matched budgets: the same tests, the same number of messages, and only the content of a message changes. This entry runs it for Luna (amendment, fixed before the runs).

Configuration

Three message conditions. Everything else is the same: the world, δ = 1/64, one test per cell, one message per generation and 24 generations, stated in the prompt from the start. The rare error is used because there only a few cells find the counterexample, so the outcome turns on whether it spreads. The run is 24 generations because in entry 3 rare-error runs needed until generation 16–22 to finish.

conditionwhat a message carries
rule onlythe key of the rule the cell holds
rule + chosen resultthat key, and one test result from memory if the model adds it
rule + attached resultthat key, and the engine attaches the latest result against HF
  • The engine attaches a result only when the cell has one that contradicts HF: the most recent one in its memory, its own or received.
  • In the third condition the sender's prompt is the "rule only" prompt, word for word. The sender is not told that a result will be attached, and a receiver cannot tell an attached result from a chosen one.
  • The attach rule reads only HF, the rule every cell starts with. It never uses the true rule, so the engine adds nothing the sender does not already hold: it only takes the decision to share out of the model's hands.
  • One run per condition, 2,400 calls each, with separate caches.

Reading

  1. A rule name from one neighbour does not move a cell. In the "rule only" run, three cells found the error, left HF and named another rule to their neighbours for 9, 16 and 23 generations. A cell on HF heard a neighbour name another rule in 332 cases, almost always from one neighbour of its eight, and left HF in one of them, for one generation. Entry 5 shows that names from a majority of neighbours do move it.
  2. A counterexample from one neighbour does. Of the cells that first received a counterexample while on HF, 74 of 91 left HF within two generations when sharing was the model's choice, and 90 of 96 when the engine attached it. Across the three runs, a cell with no counterexample in its memory left HF in 1 of 3,013 cases.
  3. The gap is not a difference in discovery. The "rule only" run had 3 finders and the "attached" run had 4.
  4. Luna shares enough on its own. When a publishing cell held a counterexample, it added one to 46 % of its messages. That run is slower at first than the attached run (10 against 46 cells at generation 6) and level with it by generation 12.

Limits: one run per condition and one model, with no hypothesis test. In the "rule only" run the finders mostly named a neighbouring rule that fits their single counterexample as well as the true rule does; the true rule itself was named in 106 of the 332 cases. In 299 of them only one of the eight neighbours named another rule, so this run shows that one name of eight does not move Luna; it does not show what several names would do; entry 5 tests that. The same three conditions are now running on gpt-oss-20b at δ = 1/8, where cells find counterexamples but rarely share them.

5 · Rule only, when many neighbours name the rule (Luna)

2026-11-16descriptive

In entry 4 a cell almost never heard another rule from more than one neighbour, so that run tested one dose. This entry repeats the "rule only" condition where the error is common (δ = 1/8) and many cells find it, so that cells without evidence of their own hear another rule from several neighbours (amendment, with the measures, reference levels and readings fixed before the run).

Configuration

  • The same model, prompt and settings as the "rule only" run of entry 4, with δ = 1/8, one test per cell, 24 generations, one run.
  • A cell is "without evidence" while it has no test result that contradicts HF. No results travel in messages, so only its own test can give it one.
  • For each such cell on HF, we count the neighbours that named another rule in the previous generation, and whether the cell then left HF.

Results

All 100 cells held the true rule by generation 9. Of them, 67 found a counterexample with their own test, and 33 never had one.

"Naming neighbours" are those of the cell's eight neighbours that named a rule other than HF in the previous generation. A case is one cell in one generation, on HF and without evidence. The amendment fixed the rows 0, 1, 2, 3 and "4 or more"; the split of the last row was made after seeing the data.

Reading

  1. Rule names do move Luna, at a high dose. The amendment's test of this was the rate at three or more naming neighbours: 37 of 99 cases, with a lower bound of 0.27 against a reference of 0.021 from entry 4. The 33 cells that never had a counterexample all ended on the true rule.
  2. The response is a step at the majority. With up to four of eight neighbours naming another rule, no cell left HF in 141 cases. With five or more, 37 of 41 did. This split was found after seeing the data.
  3. This is what separates a name from a counterexample. In entry 4 a counterexample from a single neighbour moved 74 of 91 cells within two generations. A name needs five. Where the error is rare, few cells find it, a majority of naming neighbours never forms, and only shared evidence can carry the population.
  4. The comparison fixed in advance is close to its boundary. Of the cells first exposed to three or more naming neighbours, 20 of 38 left HF within two generations (interval 0.34–0.71). That interval touches the evidence level from entry 4 (0.70–0.90), so by the rule written before the run a name at this dose counts as "about as strong as a counterexample". The step in point 2 shows why the figure is mixed: three naming neighbours do nothing, five do almost everything.

Limits: one run and one model. A cell appears in several cases, so the case counts are not independent. Intervals are exact 97.5 % intervals, two comparisons with a Bonferroni correction. The majority step matches how this model responded to rule names in the earlier Constitutional Life experiments, where no test is available at all.

Limits: one run per condition, with no hypothesis test. In the "chosen result" run 10 cells went back from the true rule to HF in the last generation (72 cells at generation 23, 62 at generation 24); we have not explained this.

7 · Main phase, Luna: repeated runs, tests fixed in advance

2026-11-18tests fixed in advance

Luna · δ 1/64 · B 1 · rule only / + chosen result / + attached result, 4 runs each · δ 1/8 · B 1 · rule only, 5 runs · 24 generations · world 0 · a cell may also send nothing

Entries 4 and 5 had one run per condition. One run cannot tell a difference between conditions from the spread between runs of the same condition: in entries 2 and 3, two Luna runs of one cell ended generation 12 with 32 and 55 cells on HT. This entry repeats Luna's conditions: four new runs of each message condition at δ = 1/64, and five new runs of "rule only" at δ = 1/8 (amendment, with the measure, the tests and the predictions fixed before the first call). The runs of entries 4 and 5 are not part of any test.

Configuration

  • Which conditions, and why.
    • The three message conditions of entry 4 (rule only, + chosen result, + attached result) at δ = 1/64. With a rare error only a few cells find the counterexample, so the outcome turns on whether it spreads, which is the question. Four new runs each, runs 2–5.
    • Rule only at δ = 1/8, the condition of entry 5. With a common error most cells find it (67 of 100 in entry 5), so cells without evidence hear another rule from many neighbours at once, which is what a test of the majority step needs. Five new runs, runs 2–6.
    • Run 1 of each condition is the run of entry 4 or 5. What we found there, the majority step in particular, was found after seeing those data, so run 1 is shown beside the new runs but is not used in any test.
    • Everything else is as in entries 4 and 5: one test per cell for the whole run (each cell has one chance to find the counterexample itself), 24 generations, the same prompts and settings. 17 runs, 40,800 decisions.
  • What a repeat varies. Two things in this setup are random. The world: HF, the 100 base rules and the value of δ are fixed by design. A world seed draws the rest: the 16 substitution rules of the catalog and which of them is HT, so also the region of inputs where HF and HT differ; the rule keys; each cell's two examples; the order of the catalog lines in each prompt; and the signals of generation 0. Every run on this page uses world seed 0. The language model's sampling: every cell's decision is a separate call to Luna, and Luna samples each answer, so the same prompt can get a different test input, message or rule. This holds in all three message conditions alike; the conditions only change what a message may carry. This entry repeats the sampling and keeps the world fixed. Every run starts from the same generation-1 prompts, byte for byte those of entries 4 and 5; from generation 2 on, each run's prompts follow its own history. We set no sampling seed and send none to the model, and every run has its own answer cache, so no answer is shared between runs. A repeat over world seeds, with another hidden region and other examples in every cell, is a separate experiment and has not been run.
  • The run is the unit. Cells in a run hear each other, so their decisions are not independent observations; 100 cells of one run are not 100 samples. Every test therefore compares run values, and the cell counts inside a run are only descriptive.
  • Measure for the message conditions: x̄, the mean share of the 100 cells on HT over generations 13–24, one number per run. The second half is used so that the early spread is over, and twelve generations are averaged so that a swing in one generation does not decide a run (in entry 6 one run lost 10 cells in its last generation). x̄ counts every cell on HT, whether it found the counterexample itself or was moved by neighbours.
  • Test for the message conditions: an exact permutation test. The eight x̄ values of two conditions can be split into two groups of four in 70 ways; p is the share of splits whose first group is at least as high as the observed one. The smallest possible p is therefore 1/70 = 0.014. There are three comparisons, held at 0.05 together (Bonferroni), so each needs p ≤ 0.0167, which only complete separation gives: every run of one condition above every run of the other. Four runs is the fewest that can pass: with three against three the smallest p is 1/20 = 0.05.
  • Test for the majority step: in each run, take the cells on HF with no counterexample of their own (a cell with one is moved by its own evidence, not by names). A cell stays exposed for several generations, so it is counted once in each group: at its first generation with one to four naming neighbours, and at its first with five or more. The share that left HF at that generation is compared within the run. The step holds if the share at five or more is higher in every run. If the runs carried no step, each would come out higher with probability at most 1/2, so all five with probability at most 1/32 = 0.031. Five runs is the fewest that can pass: with four the bound is 1/16 = 0.0625. The cut at five neighbours was found in entry 5 and fixed before these runs.
  • One deviation: an internet outage stopped the last dose run in its first generation. It was resumed with the same requests, and the 28 answers received before the outage were replayed from the stored answers.

Reading

  1. A rule name does not carry a rare error, in any run. In each "rule only" run two to six cells found the counterexample with their own test, and no other cell reached the true rule.
  2. A counterexample does, whenever someone finds one. With results allowed in messages, every run held all or almost all cells on the true rule in the second half, including two runs where a single cell had found the counterexample before anyone shared one. With attached results, the three runs that had a finder reached 0.82–1.00, and every cell that reached the true rule without its own counterexample had first seen a shared one.
  3. The failed prediction is about finding, not spreading. In run 5 of the attached condition no cell tested an input where the two rules differ (0 of 96 tests), so there was nothing to attach and every cell stayed on HF. In the eight runs that share this prompt ("rule only" and attached results) such tests were 27 of 790 (3.4 %), so a run without one has a chance of about 3 %. By the rule fixed in advance, L2 does not hold. The difference of means is +0.70, with the attached runs ranging 0–1.00 and the "rule only" runs 0–0.012. This explanation was found after seeing the data.
  4. Sharing does not make cells better at finding. Before any counterexample reached them, cells tested an input where the rules differ in 16 of 394 tests with rule only, 8 of 348 with chosen results and 5 of 351 with attached results. After receiving one, cells allowed to share tested such inputs in 33 of 51 tests, mostly not the input they had received; with attached results, in 6 of 45. So the gap in L1 is the spread of evidence, not more discovery. This split was also made after seeing the data.
  5. The majority step of entry 5 repeats. Over the five runs, a cell without evidence left HF in 1 of 330 cases with one to four naming neighbours, and in 166 of 183 with five or more.

Limits: one model and one world, four or five runs per condition. The tests treat a run as the unit; counts of cells inside a run are not independent. The same repeats for gpt-oss-20b (entry 6) are running.

Where the true rule comes from

Each world's catalog also lists the simpler sibling of HT: the same substitution without its condition, call it U (it is the δ = 1/8 rule of that world). A cell that finds one counterexample cannot tell U from HT: its two examples and its one counterexample fit both. To rule U out it needs a different result, an input where U predicts the substitution and none happens. The counts below come from the seven runs with chosen results at δ = 1/64 (this entry's four and runs 3–5 of entry 7), and were made after seeing the data.

  • With rule names only, finders settle on U. All nine finders in the four rule-only runs above moved to U, not to HT; one world-0 cell tried HT for seven generations late in the run and went back to U. With one test per cell, their only result is the counterexample, so nothing they hold rules U out. What their neighbours hear from them is U's name.
  • The first finder picks U; a name picks among rules that fit. Across all Luna runs at δ = 1/64 (entries 2–3, 7 and 8), take the cells that found a counterexample before receiving one. When no neighbour had yet named HT, 34 of 49 took U and 11 took HT. When a neighbour had named HT, 36 of 39 took HT. With evidence of its own, a name decides between rules that fit it; without evidence, a name below a majority almost never moves a cell (entries 5 and 7). In the rule-only runs of entries 7 and 8 the first finders took U, so HT was never named and later finders had nothing to follow.
  • With results, a finder moves on once U is ruled out by someone else. Of 20 cells that found a counterexample before receiving one, 12 first took U and 7 went straight to HT. All 20 ended on HT, each in or after the generation in which a neighbour's result ruling out U reached it.
  • The two pieces come from different cells. Of the 700 cells that reached HT, 688 held both a counterexample to HF and a result ruling out U at the moment they moved.
  • One piece is rare, the other common. Luna aims its tests at the substitutions in the catalog: before any counterexample reached them, 35–41 % of cells' tests (41 % with rule names only, 35 % with results) fell where U and HF differ but HT and HF do not (10.9 % for a random input), and 3.2–3.4 % on HT's own region (1.6 % at random). Every such test returns HF's output and so rules U out, and these results are shared often (117–209 such messages per run). The counterexample is the scarce piece.

So no cell holds the evidence for HT at first. A rare counterexample against the starting rule and a common negative result against its simpler rival are found by different cells, and the population reaches the true rule only when both can travel. In the rule-only runs the second piece exists, in the cells that tested U's region, but is never sent.

Majority step across worlds

Rule only at δ = 1/8 in worlds 1–4, with run 2 of entry 7 for world 0, tested as in entry 7: the step holds if, in every world, cells without evidence leave HF more often at five or more naming neighbours than at one to four (p ≤ 1/32 if each world were a coin toss). Prediction: holds.

Where the tests go

Of 328 finders, 292 held HT two generations after their counterexample, and only 8 held U; 233 of 310 by then held a result of their own that rules U out. The tests explain the jump in finders. Counted after seeing the data, by what the tester knew when it chose the test:

Entries 4–9 compare channels that carry rule names, with or without results. None of them has a channel that carries nothing, so what the names add on their own was not measured. Here no message reaches any cell, in any generation (amendment, fixed before the first call). The comparison is the rule-only runs at δ = 1/8 in the same worlds (entry 7 run 2 for world 0, entry 8 for worlds 1–3). The same split, a team that cannot talk between one agent and a team that can, is used by the Multi Agent Coordination Bench.

Configuration

  • Silent: the prompt, schema and settings of rule only. Every neighbour line reads as for a neighbour that sent nothing. Cells still write messages; these are stored and never delivered. The cells are not told that nothing is delivered.
  • Test: x̄ with rule names above x̄ silent, four worlds against four, one claim at 0.05 (the unpaired permutation test of entries 8 and 9, an approximation over the same worlds). Prediction: holds.
  • One deviation, made before any result was read: the silent runs cost more per call than projected, so the last world could not start under the spending stop; the stop was raised once, by an addendum, and the run was completed.

Reading

  • Without messages only the finders get there. No cell reached the true rule without a counterexample of its own (x̄nf = 0 in every world), so this setup has no guessing floor.
  • Names add the other half of the population, all of it cells without evidence, through the majority step of entries 5, 7 and 8. The number of finders is about the same with and without names.
  • Put together for Luna: with a common error, names carry the error from the finders to the rest; with a rare error, names alone carry it only when a cell can still test (entry 9), and results carry it with one test (entries 7 and 8).
  • Cells that hear nothing reason longer: 315 reasoning tokens per call on average, against 197 with rule names. They still write a message in 85–87 % of their turns, against 99 % with names.

Limits: one model, four worlds, one run each. The silent condition was run at δ = 1/8 only; at δ = 1/64 rule names alone already stay near zero. The same comparison for gpt-oss-20b is queued on the GPU.

Reading

  1. Nemotron hardly tests. With four tests per cell it used 17–19 of 400, and with one test 10–17 of 100. The few tests it ran at δ = 1/8 with B = 4 landed on the rare inputs 35 % of the time, above a random tester's 12.5 %, but on 17 tests.
  2. It never passes a result on. None of its 4,800 messages carried a result. It was silent in 60–64 % of its turns, and the rest named a rule.
  3. The few cells that found the error moved. Every cell that received a counterexample, its own, left HF within two generations; one of six at δ = 1/8 with B = 4 later went back. With no evidence passed on, nobody else followed.
  4. Nothing spread, by either channel. Finders rarely named their new rule: 1–13 messages per run named a rule other than HF, the rest were silence or HF. Every cell off HF at generation 12 was a finder, except one cell on an unrelated rule at δ = 1/64, B = 1. Cells without a counterexample of their own did leave HF (3–8 per run), but all except that one came back. Three profiles across the models so far: Luna passes evidence on and follows a majority of names; gpt-oss-20b keeps its evidence and ignores names; Nemotron under this budget hardly searches, and a finding stays with its finder. These counts were made after seeing the data.
  5. The budget cut more than it was derived for. It closed the reasoning of 176 of 4,800 calls (3.7 %), not only the runaway ones: reasoning that ended on its own reached 14,974 tokens. The closed calls are spread over all generations, including the first, before any result exists, so the budget did not mainly cut moments of evidence. It did cut moments of change: a closed call changed the cell's rule in 25 of 176 cases (14 %), against 1.2 % of all decisions. Long reasoning here is a search through the catalog, and the budget ended some of those searches.

Limits: one run per cell, under a thinking budget set for this model. All numbers are descriptive.

18 · Does gpt-oss-20b choose informative tests?

2026-11-23tests fixed in advance

gpt-oss-20b · every test in 26 runs already shown: entries 11 (δ 1/8, world 0, three message conditions, runs 2–5), 13 (δ 1/8, worlds 1–3) and 17 (δ 1/64, B 4, worlds 0–3) · no new model calls

The entries above ask whether evidence spreads. This one asks whether a cell, given what its prompt shows, picks a test that can tell its live rules apart (amendment, fixed before any test was scored; after Amayuelas et al., arXiv 2611.10501). For each test: V is the set of catalog rules that fit everything the cell had seen; a test input splits V if those rules disagree on it; its information is the entropy of that split. The chosen test is ranked among all 4,096 inputs the cell could have chosen, so a uniform pick has mean rank 0.5. The run is the unit.

  • T-C1: mean rank above 0.5 in at least 18 of the 26 runs. T-C2: the chosen test splits V more often than a uniform pick, same rule. No prediction was stated.

Results

testruns above chancepresult
T-C1, information rank12 / 260.72does not hold
T-C2, splits the live rules9 / 260.96does not hold

By the reading fixed in advance: its chosen tests are no more informative than a uniform pick. All 14 world-0 runs are below chance on both measures; the 12 runs above chance are all in worlds 1–3. A uniform pick splits V with probability 0.75 on average, so the measures had room.

Reading

  1. Two favourite inputs decide the world split. 43 % of its tests are AAAA or ABCD, whatever the cell has seen. In world 0 these almost never separate the live rules (they split V in 6 % of cases); in worlds 1–3 they often do. Its other tests are above chance in every world (mean rank 0.61–0.74).
  2. Hearing HT named moves its tests, as in entry 17: after a neighbour named HT, 59–85 % of its tests at δ 1/8 fall on HT's region.
  3. Luna, for comparison (not part of the test): its tests are above chance in all 35 of its runs, mean rank 0.57–0.90.

Limits: points 1–3 are counted after the data. Information is measured with every fitting rule weighted equally, a convention, not the model's belief. The reviewer recomputed every test in all 26 runs from the stored traces.

Claude Haiku 5.5 · part S: δ 1/8 · B 1 · no message delivered, against rule only (entry 19) · part L: δ 1/64 · B 4 against B 1 · rule only · 24 generations · worlds 0–3, one run per world and condition

Entry 19 showed that for Claude Haiku 5.5 rule names alone moved almost no cell without its own counterexample (x̄nf ≤ 0.004). Two questions follow, both asked before for other models: do names add anything over silence (entry 10 for Luna, entry 15 for gpt-oss-20b), and do four tests per cell raise the share on HT of a rare error (entry 9 for Luna, entry 17 for gpt-oss-20b)? Prompts, schemas and engine as before; only the model changed (amendment, fixed before the first call). The rule-only runs of part S are the four runs of entry 19, compared by file hash, not rerun.

  • Test T-SH: x̄ with rule names above x̄ silent, four worlds against four, p ≤ 3/70 needed. Prediction: does not hold, because in entry 19 no cell without a counterexample of its own reached HT, so names and silence should differ only through finders.
  • Test T-H4: x̄ with four tests above x̄ with one, rule only, δ 1/64. Prediction: holds, because four tests put more cells on the region, so finders alone raise x̄ above the one-test runs.

Reading

  1. Rule names add nothing over silence for this model. In both conditions x̄ is close to the number of finders divided by 100, and no cell without its own counterexample reached HT. Unlike Luna (entry 9) and gpt-oss-20b (entry 15), names do not move Haiku's tests toward the region either: 100 of 400 tests on the region silent, 92 of 400 with names. Counted after the data.
  2. Four tests add finders, and only finders. 15 cells found a counterexample with four tests against 1 with one. No other cell followed them, although one to five cells named HT in most generations. For Luna with the same setting, names alone carried the error to 0.31–0.99 of the grid (entry 9).
  3. A finder may land on the wrong rule. At δ 1/64 a counterexample fits both HT and the unconditional substitution (HT at δ 1/8). Two generations after its first counterexample, a finder named HT in 8 cases of 15, the unconditional substitution in 6 and HF in 1. Counted after the data.
  4. The tests are not aimed at the region. 22 of 1,595 tests with B 4 landed on it (1.4 %; a random tester: 1/64 = 1.6 %). Counted after the data.

Limits: one model, four worlds, one run each; part S compares new runs with entry 19's runs of the same day. Points 1, 3 and 4 are counted after the data. In the viewer, the unconditional substitution shows as "other rule". The runs are in the run viewer under Claude Haiku 5.5.

Reading

Limits: one model, four worlds, one run each. The runs are in the run viewer under Core experiments, Four tests, Claude Haiku 5.5.

Single cells in isolation

The entries above are population runs: a hundred cells find, update, pass on and act on evidence together, so a difference between models cannot be placed at one step. Here one cell at a time gets a counterexample it did not have to find, with no population around it. Same prompts for every model.

16 · Does a cell update on a counterexample, and does it pass it on?

2026-11-22 · 11-25readings fixed in advance

Luna, gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b, Claude Haiku 5.5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (thinking capped at 7,168 tokens, answer forced) · δ 1/8 · B 1, already spent · rule plus a chosen result · world 0 · one cell, generation 6 · 20 cells × 3 conditions × 3 draws

Each prompt is a single cell in generation 6 of a QX-3 run that never happened. It previously named HF, all eight neighbours named HF in generation 5, and its one test is spent. Its memory holds exactly one result of its own and one result received from the neighbour on its first inbox slot; that neighbour still names HF, as a cell that only relays would. Only which of the two results is the counterexample changes:

conditionown resultreceived result
U0 · controlAAAA → BBBBCAAA → DBBB
U1 · own counterexampleDAAA → FBBBAAAA → BBBB
U2 · received counterexampleAAAA → BBBBDAAA → FBBB

AAAA → BBBB and CAAA → DBBB fit both HF and HT; DAAA → FBBB contradicts HF, which gives EBBB. With it, only HT and two other catalog rules fit a cell's evidence. U1 and U2 hold the same two results with the source swapped.

  • Measures (cell is the unit, three draws per cell): consistent, the named rule fits all the cell's evidence; leave, it is not HF; attaches the counterexample, the message carries DAAA → FBBB. 95 % intervals resample the 20 cells.
  • Readings fixed in advance: U1 low → it does not update; U1 high and U2 clearly lower → it discounts the same evidence from a neighbour; U1 high and few counterexamples passed on → it does not share; none of these → no bottleneck in isolation.

Consistent, U2 − U1 by cell, 95 % interval: Luna −0.22 [−0.33, −0.10]; gpt-oss-120b −0.43 [−0.58, −0.28]; gpt-oss-20b −0.05 [−0.20, 0.12]; Qwen3.6 −0.08 [−0.22, +0.05]. Of the answers that update, the counterexample is passed on in 54 of 59 and 41 of 46 (Luna, U1 and U2), 21 of 52 and 10 of 26 (gpt-oss-120b), 3 of 30 and 0 of 27 (gpt-oss-20b), 42 of 52 and 28 of 47 (Qwen3.6). Qwen3.6 rows: thinking capped at 7,168 tokens; 237 of its 240 world-0 answers reached the cap and were forced.

Reading

By the readings fixed in advance, one per model. The amendment set no number for "high" or "low"; the reading names the comparison it rests on.

  1. Luna updates on its own counterexample (59 of 60) and less often on the same counterexample from a neighbour (46 of 60): consistent with a source bottleneck. When it updates, it shares the evidence nine times in ten.
  2. gpt-oss-120b shows the same pattern, stronger: 52 of 60 on its own counterexample, 26 of 60 on a received one. When it updates, it attaches the counterexample in about two answers of five; otherwise it names its new rule without the evidence. With a received counterexample it more often attaches its own result that fits HF (22 of its 32 attachments in U2).
  3. gpt-oss-20b, in world 0, updates on only half its own counterexamples (30 of 60), and about as often on a received one (27 of 60); the source makes no measurable difference there (worlds 1–3 below differ). Every answer that does not update keeps HF but one. Against Luna's 59 of 60, this is read as consistent with an updating bottleneck. It also shares least: when it updates it names its new rule without the evidence (28 of 60 in U1) and attaches the counterexample in 3 of 30; it is silent in about one turn in eight, and in 19 of 60 turns with nothing to report (U0).
  4. Passing evidence on and using it come apart in both directions. Two Luna answers pass the counterexample on while still naming HF; many gpt-oss answers name the new rule and keep the evidence that would let a neighbour check it.
  5. What U2 − U1 does not separate. In U2 the neighbour sends the counterexample but still names HF: the evidence arrives with its sender's own vote against it, and in a message rather than in the cell's memory. The difference therefore does not show distrust of neighbours as such.

Answers whose rule fits all the cell's evidence. No model left HF without a counterexample (U0) in any world. T-U3: Luna +0.23 [+0.14, +0.32], holds, as predicted; Haiku +0.03 [−0.01, +0.06], does not hold (prediction uncertain); gpt-oss-20b +0.05 [−0.04, +0.14], does not hold, against the prediction; gpt-oss-120b +0.17 [+0.08, +0.25], holds (prediction uncertain); Qwen3.6 +0.27 [+0.20, +0.33], holds (prediction uncertain). Pooled over the four worlds, Luna's U3 stays below its U1: −0.26 [−0.34, −0.18]; Qwen3.6's is above it: +0.17 [+0.11, +0.22].

  1. Luna: both effects, and world 0 was the mildest. In every world it updates far less on a received counterexample than on its own (U2 − U1 from −0.22 in world 0 to −0.73 in world 1). When the sender also names HT, updating rises in every world, yet stays below its own-evidence level. By the readings fixed in advance: the sender's named rule matters, and received evidence is still taken less than its own. Luna still passes the counterexample on in 9 of 10 updating answers in every condition.
  2. Claude Haiku 5.5 updates on a counterexample almost whatever its source: 238 of 240 on its own, 224 of 240 received, 230 of 240 with the sender naming HT; only world 1 shows a drop for a received one. It shares the evidence least of the strong models: of its updating answers, a third attach the counterexample with its own (80 of 238), a fifth with a received one (41 of 224); most name the new rule alone, and about one turn in eleven is silent.
  1. gpt-oss-20b: world 0 was its hardest world, and the source does matter elsewhere. On its own counterexample it updates in 48, 43 and 29 of 60 in worlds 1–3 (30 in world 0). On a received one it updates clearly less in worlds 1–3 (U2 − U1 −0.40, −0.45, −0.28, intervals below 0), which world 0 did not show. A sender naming HT does not raise it overall (T-U3 does not hold): by the readings fixed in advance, the drop is about the source or the channel, not the sender's named rule. In isolation it never passes on a counterexample it received (0 of 79 updating answers in U2, 1 of 91 in U3) and rarely its own (22 of 150).
  2. gpt-oss-120b repeats Luna's pattern in every world. A received counterexample is taken less often than its own (U2 − U1 from −0.20 to −0.43, all intervals below 0); a sender naming HT raises it (T-U3 holds), and it stays below its own level (U3 − U1, pooled, −0.13 [−0.19, −0.08]). When it updates, it attaches the counterexample in about half of its own cases (98 of 208) and a fifth to a third of received ones (28 of 136; 52 of 176).
  3. Qwen3.6, with its thinking capped, names a rule that fits more often when the sender names HT than when the counterexample is its own (227 against 187 of 240; U3 − U1 above 0 in every world). A received counterexample with the sender on HF is taken a little less than its own (163 of 240; pooled U2 − U1 −0.10 [−0.16, −0.04], in world 1 alone below 0). T-U3 holds, but with U3 above U1, a pattern none of the readings fixed in advance covers. It passes the counterexample on in 136 of 187 updating answers with its own, 90 of 163 with a received one, and 71 of 227 when the sender names HT: there it mostly names HT without the result. Answers that do not fit keep the world's HF. 936 of its 960 answers reached the 7,168-token cap and were forced; of the 24 that ended their thinking earlier, 12 of the 13 outside U0 kept HF.

Next

  • Main phase on local models, gpt-oss-20b and then Qwen3-4B-Thinking. It covers the full grid of δ and B, with predictions fixed against the scripted references before any call.
